svg.aria-label: Diagram: how an AWS CloudHSM cluster backup is encrypted, what is required to restore it, and what the retention policy does and does not cover. CloudHSM makes periodic backups of the users, keys and policies in the cluster and stores them in a service-controlled Amazon S3 bucket in the same region as the cluster, with a 99.999999999 percent durability level, the same as any object stored in Amazon S3. The bucket being service-controlled means it is not in the customer's account, so there is no bucket policy, object lock or lifecycle rule the customer can apply, and the retention policy is the only available lifecycle control. The encryption chain is documented in detail. When CloudHSM makes a backup from the HSM, the HSM encrypts all of its data before sending it, and the data never leaves the HSM in plaintext form. The HSM uses an ephemeral backup key, an AES 256-bit key generated inside the HSM at backup time, to encrypt the data. That ephemeral key is itself encrypted by a persistent backup key, also AES 256-bit, which is derived rather than stored. The inputs to the derivation include a manufacturer key backup key permanently embedded in the HSM hardware by the hardware manufacturer, and an AWS key backup key securely installed in the HSM when it is initially configured by CloudHSM. Two consequences follow, and together they are the central point of the post. First, backups cannot be decrypted by AWS, because AWS does not have access to the key used to decrypt the backups, which is the property that justifies choosing CloudHSM when AWS technical access is unacceptable. Second, CloudHSM can restore backups onto only AWS-owned HSMs made by the same manufacturer, because the derivation inputs exist only inside such hardware. The backup is therefore confidential from AWS and simultaneously unusable without AWS. It is not a file that can be taken elsewhere but a restore ticket valid at one vendor, so a disaster recovery plan must not treat restoring the backup somewhere else as a fallback; genuine vendor independence requires exported keys under the customer's own wrapping, which is a different design to be chosen deliberately. There is also an outer encryption layer: a backup consists of only encrypted data, and before the service stores it in S3 the service encrypts the backup again using AWS Key Management Service. The outer layer is the one AWS can manage and the one that appears in KMS key policies and CloudTrail, and it is not the layer protecting the key material. On restore semantics, because each backup contains all users, keys and configuration from the original HSM, the restored HSM contains the same protections and access controls as the original, so a restore rolls back user and quorum configuration as well as key material and can reinstate a crypto officer removed since the backup. The restored data overwrites all other data that might have been on the HSM prior to restoration, so there is no merge and anything created since the backup timestamp is lost. On lifecycle, CloudHSM purges backups based on the retention policy set when a cluster is created, and that policy applies to clusters rather than to backups. The finding worth acting on is that if a backup is moved to a different region it is no longer associated with a cluster and has no backup retention policy, and the customer must manually delete any backups not associated with a cluster. The cross-Region copy made for resilience therefore leaves the lifecycle entirely: it is never purged, has no expiry, and because CloudTrail reports backups marked for deletion and nothing marks this one it does not appear there either, while still containing all users, keys and configuration from the original HSM. So the most carefully protected copy and the least governed copy are produced by the same resilience decision. The retention period can be set to any number between 7 and 379 days. Clusters created before November 18, 2020 have a retention policy of 90 days plus the age of the cluster, with AWS's own example being a cluster created on November 18, 2019 receiving one year plus 90 days, that is 455 days. CloudHSM does not delete a cluster's last backup, which is a deliberate floor preventing a misconfigured policy from destroying key material. After a backup is explicitly deleted the service holds it for seven days during which it can be restored, after which it can no longer be restored, and the backup moves to the PENDING_DELETE state, which makes the grace period queryable. To prevent a race condition, the retention policy for a cluster should be changed before restoring a backup that the service deleted. Managed backup retention can be opted out of altogether by contacting AWS Support. Finally, before a cluster can be deleted all HSMs must be removed from it, which means deleting a cluster is not a single call that an over-broad automation could make by accident. The recommended audit is to list every backup with no cluster association, since that set has no retention policy, no expiry and no deletion record while each member contains all users, keys and configuration from the original HSM, and then to read the disaster recovery document for the phrase restore the backup and confirm it says into a CloudHSM cluster in an AWS Region.
svg.title: Confidential from AWS, and unusable without AWS, from the same key derivation
svg.text: Two sentences that sound contradictory and are one design decision.
AWS CloudHSM cluster backups — and the retention rule that the resilience move walks out of.
Why you chose CloudHSM
“backups cannot be decrypted by AWS
because AWS doesn't have access to key used
to decrypt the backups”
“never leaves the HSM in plaintext form”
What comes with it
“can restore backups onto only AWS-owned
HSMs made by the same manufacturer”
Not a file you can take elsewhere. A restore
ticket valid at one vendor.
Both facts fall out of one derivation — the backup key is in nobody's custody
EBK AES 256 ephemeral, “generated inside the HSM” → encrypts the data
PBK AES 256 DERIVED, not stored → encrypts the EBK
inputs: MKBK “permanently embedded… by the hardware manufacturer”
AKBK “securely installed… by AWS CloudHSM”
Reconstructible only where both exist: inside that manufacture of HSM, configured by AWS. So AWS cannot read it, and nor can anyone else.
The retention policy attaches to the cluster. The DR copy leaves the cluster.
“Backup retention policy applies to clusters.”
“If you move a backup to a different region, that backup is no longer associated with a cluster and
has no backup retention policy. You must manually delete any backups not associated with a cluster.”
Never purged. No expiry. Nothing marks it, so nothing reports it — and it holds all users, keys and configuration.
The lifecycle, where it applies
retention range 7 – 379 days
pre-2020 clusters 365 + 90 = 455 days
after you delete 7 days to restore
last backup never purged
A floor, a grace period, a queryable state — all
A restore is a rollback, not a merge
“the restored HSM contains the same
protections and access controls as the original”
“overwrites all other data that might have been
on the HSM prior to restoration”
A removed crypto officer comes back with it.
expressed in terms of a cluster the standalone copy no longer belongs to.
The audit
List every backup with no cluster association — that set is exactly what nothing is managing. Then read your DR doc
for “restore the backup”; if it does not say “into a CloudHSM cluster in an AWS Region”, it assumes a capability you lack.
Nothing here is broken. The lifecycle simply has no noun to hang on once the backup stands alone, and AWS says so.
